question.prompt:
Let \(@\) denote the “averaged with” operation: \(a @ b = \frac{a+b}{2}.\) Which of the following distributive laws hold for all numbers \(x,\) \(y,\) and \(z?\)

I. \(x @ (y + z) = (x @ y) + (x @ z)\)

II. \(x + (y @ z) = (x + y) @ (x + z)\)

III. \(x @ (y @ z) = (x @ y) @ (x @ z)\)

solutions.explanation:
Replace each occurrence of \(@\) by the average of its two inputs. A true law must give equal expressions for arbitrary \(x,y,z\); one counterexample is enough to disprove a law.

For I, the two sides are
\[
x@(y+z)=\frac{x+y+z}{2}
\]
and
\[
(x@y)+(x@z)
=\frac{x+y}{2}+\frac{x+z}{2}
=\frac{2x+y+z}{2}.
\]
They are not always equal. For instance, \(x=2\) and \(y=z=0\) give \(1\) on the left and \(2\) on the right. Thus I is false.

For II, expanding the right side gives
\[
(x+y)@(x+z)
=\frac{(x+y)+(x+z)}2
=x+\frac{y+z}{2}
=x+(y@z).
\]
Thus II holds for all inputs.

For III, the left side is
\[
x@(y@z)
=\frac{x+(y+z)/2}{2}
=\frac{2x+y+z}{4}.
\]
The right side is
\[
(x@y)@(x@z)
=\frac{(x+y)/2+(x+z)/2}{2}
=\frac{2x+y+z}{4}.
\]
Thus III also holds for all inputs. All denominators are the nonzero constants \(2\) or \(4\), so these calculations impose no extra restrictions. The answer is \(\boxed{\text{II and III only}}\), choice E.
solutions.title: Replace each operation by its definition
